Guidry 1

#### Abstract:

Wetlands are protected, managed, and restored worldwide to provide a range of ecosystem services, including (i) habitat for plants and animals, (ii) carbon storage, (iii) improving downstream water quality, and (iv) reducing flooding by river and coastal waters. When did such conservation begin, and how do early conservation efforts shape recent public policy? This thesis identifies some of the earliest recorded examples of private efforts in Louisiana and analyzes how these early efforts shaped State and Federal Government action in the realm of conservation. The earliest wetland protection efforts in Louisiana began in the 1910s to sustain continental populations of migratory birds. By 1921, over 170,000 acres were donated to the state government by wealthy Americans nationwide. The actions by several of these individuals fit the mold of what we would now classify as a policy entrepreneur. After beginning as an endeavor led by wealthy individuals, conservation efforts shifted to government-led conservation at the state and national level, with the creation of wetland management areas and state and national bureaucracies dedicated to management. Policy at the state and federal level in the 1980s, including legislation and funding, appears to have been catalyzed by a coalition of private citizens acting as policy entrepreneurs representing interests ranging from those of commercial fishers in coastal Louisiana to national organizations interested in wildlife conservation.

#### Introduction:

Louisiana, USA, stands out in its capability to utilize and capitalize on abundant natural resources. Dedicating billions of dollars toward wetland conservation efforts, the Louisiana state government and the federal government constitute an environmental protection regime that was unimaginable a century ago. The ever-expanding roles of the state and federal government raise a serious question for Louisianians and conservationists elsewhere: how did Louisiana accomplish this? The origins of Louisiana’s coastal wetland conservation efforts deserve to be explored because conservation of its extensive coastal wetlands, estimated at 3.6 million acres with broad environmental gradients [(1) Brady et al. 2017], may have produced more archival and sources than elsewhere. Conserving wetlands, and coastal wetlands in particular, is not unique to Louisiana but rather is a globally significant activity that reflects an important relationship between people and the environment. When did such conservation begin? In Louisiana coastal wetlands, [(2) Killebrew & Khalil (2018)] described a pattern in which wetland conservation began in 1981 with state law creating a $35 million trust fund, a 1989 state law creating new permanent funding, and a 1990 federal law that was the first national mandate for action and for federal funding for coastal wetland restoration in the United States.

Guidry 2

This paper will describe the efforts of private citizens, which served as a catalyst for subsequent government action. The actions of these individuals will be examined using the modern literature that defines policy entrepreneurs in terms of their initiative and actions that seek to shape the public policy action of governments. The origins of coastal wetland conservation are firmly rooted in the actions of these wealthy policy entrepreneurs who helped spur and shape the transition to government-sponsored conservation efforts. These efforts are documented using primary sources and scholarly journals that detail individual, state, and federal involvement. We show that the origins of Louisiana’s coastal wetland conservation efforts can be traced back a century to the desires of wealthy private citizens, who had a vested interest in preserving and protecting migratory bird and game populations for hunting and conservation purposes. Then, through an outline of a general definition of what a policy entrepreneur is, along with key characteristics, we will show the parallels of private citizens' actions to those most associated with policy entrepreneurship. We note a transition from being led by wealthy individuals to being led by the state wildlife agency and public policy to aid their efforts through the 1970s. We then show that state and federal legislation and funding for coastal wetland conservation in the 1980s and 1990s appear to have been catalyzed by a coalition of private citizens representing interests ranging from those of commercial fishers in coastal Louisiana to those of national organizations interested in wildlife conservation. Before diving into the history of early conservation efforts and their causes, it is important to recognize the international importance of wetlands in Louisiana. The 1st Report of the Conservation Commission of Louisiana, which chronicles the efforts made in conservation from 1912 to 1914, explains why Louisiana’s conservation is critical on a national scale. It posits, “The fate of the game birds of a large portion of the North American Continent depends upon the success with which they are protected in Louisiana.” [(3) Report of Conservation Commission of Louisiana…1914] The report points out the first major efforts by private interest groups to dedicate private land towards protection. However, the main justification behind the Commission’s statement is the documented abundance of Migratory Birds throughout State Surveys, coupled with the understanding of migratory patterns and repopulation statistics, which led to the assertion of Louisiana’s importance to the migratory bird population whose life cycles span from boreal forests in Canada to tropical forests in Central and South America. The understanding was that millions of migratory birds requiring a safe haven in Louisiana for winter survival and subsequent reproduction had a direct impact locally and nationally, particularly for migratory waterfowl and other waterbirds [(3)Report of Conservation Commission of Louisiana…1914]. This idea of protection for migratory waterfowl was one that was later utilized in the creation of the Migratory Game Bird Treaty Act of 1918 between the countries of Canada, the United States of America, and Mexico. This act captures the same spirit of the above-mentioned source by applying a similar logic to that of what was expressed by those who hunted and conserved migratory birds, and applies it not only to southern and northern states, but also using the concept of protection for these animals to a multi-continental protection clause. [(4) Migratory Bird Treaty Act of 1918 1918]

Guidry 3

The 1st Report of the Conservation Commission of Louisiana also noted that the first major wetland conservation efforts, during the 1900s and 1910s, were entirely funded by private interest groups who dedicated private land towards protection. By the 2020s, wetland conservation in Louisiana was radically different. As of 2025, Louisiana plans to spend $1.71 billion on various wetland conservation, damage mitigation, and restoration projects. By then, wetland conservation had become an important governmental endeavor, and hence an important source of contracts to private industry. Similar programs focused on protecting, managing, and/or restoring wetlands now exist globally for a variety of reasons: fiber, fish and wildlife, flood protection, and carbon storage [(5) EPA’s Efforts: Coastal Wetlands Initiative]. Understanding similarities and differences in the origins and evolution of this global phenomenon is an interesting question. We offer an examination of how Louisiana’s wetland restoration developed, who started Louisiana’s wetland conservation efforts, and their motives. [(6) Fiscal year 2025 Annual Plan 2024]

#### Early Conservation and Private Citizens:

Promulgated by private citizens, the first conservation efforts in Louisiana are well documented in a letter written by Edward A. McIlhenny, submitted to the Ninth Biennial Report of the Department of Conservation of the State of Louisiana, published in 1929. McIlhenny’s letter documents the efforts made in 1893 to purchase wetlands southwest of Lafayette in Vermilion Parish. McIlhenny believed that land conservation and bird sanctuaries would be effective at his goal of wildlife conservation via private property, and as a result, he created the first-ever wild bird sanctuary in Louisiana. He coined this endeavor “Bird City,” which consisted of an artificial pond on his property that McIlhenny gave a variety of estimates on throughout the nesting season that ranged from 15,000 pairs of nesting birds at its creation, and as many as ~100,000 herons by the end of the 1911 nesting season [(7) McIlhenny 1912]. McIlhenny created this sanctuary on his land to prevent the snowy egrets it housed from, by his estimation, extermination. While the snowy egret was not a game bird, it was still severely threatened by individuals seeking to hunt the bird to satisfy demand for feathers in fashionable clothing. It signaled that conservation efforts by McIlhenny were not centered solely around game birds that he hunted for recreation but, instead, aimed at the conservation of wildlife in general. In fact, upon creating “Bird City,” McIlhenny created a film to encourage others to invest in the conservation efforts titled The Snowy Egret and Its Extermination that he self-financed and took on the cost of traveling to show others this film and encourage conservation efforts [(8) Osborn et al. 2010]. This film was even shown in a screening before Congress and was created with the intent of molding public policy towards the protection of migratory birds. It has been argued by the Institute for Community Solutions that the airing of The Snowy Egret and Its Extermination before Congress greatly influenced national legislatures to take action and pass the Migratory Bird Treaty Act of 1918 [(9) Johnson 2022]. The sanctuary was a resounding success: as McIlhenny documents, egrets returned to the sanctuary in great numbers year after year. “Bird
